title: Cloud Computing Fundamentals
summary: Compare cloud deployment models, service models, and how responsibility shifts between a provider and a customer.

nodes.label: Public · Private · Hybrid
nodes.description: A deployment model describes where cloud infrastructure runs and who can use it. Public cloud is provider-operated and broadly available; private cloud is dedicated to one organization; hybrid connects cloud and on-premises environments.
nodes.purpose: Choose the model around control, compliance, connectivity, and operating capability rather than assuming one model fits every workload.
nodes.example: A retailer keeps a latency-sensitive warehouse system locally while using public cloud analytics for aggregated inventory data.

nodes.label: IaaS
nodes.description: Infrastructure as a Service provides configurable compute, storage, and networking while the customer manages the guest operating system and application stack.
nodes.purpose: Use IaaS when a workload needs operating-system control or a migration path with fewer application changes.
nodes.example: A team moves a legacy service to a VM and remains responsible for guest patching and host-level configuration.

nodes.label: PaaS
nodes.description: Platform as a Service gives developers a managed application platform while the provider handles more operating-system and runtime operations.
nodes.purpose: Use PaaS when the application fits the platform and the team wants to focus on code, configuration, and data.
nodes.example: A web team deploys an application to App Service instead of maintaining a VM image and web server.

nodes.label: SaaS
nodes.description: Software as a Service delivers a complete application managed by its provider; customers configure users, access, and their use of the data.
nodes.purpose: Use SaaS when an existing hosted product meets the need without building and operating the application.
nodes.example: A company uses a hosted email product and manages its users and access policies rather than the mail servers.

nodes.label: Shared responsibility
nodes.description: Cloud responsibility is divided between the provider and customer, and the split changes by service model. Customers always retain responsibility for their data, identities, and access decisions.
nodes.purpose: Use the model to identify who patches, configures, protects, and monitors each layer of a solution.
nodes.example: On a VM, the customer patches the guest OS; on a managed platform, the provider operates more of the underlying host.

title: Azure Global Infrastructure
summary: Explore how Azure regions and availability zones support placement, resilience, and data-location decisions.

nodes.label: Region
nodes.description: An Azure region is a geographic area containing one or more datacenters connected through a low-latency network. Service availability differs by region.
nodes.purpose: Select a region after checking service availability, latency, resilience requirements, and applicable data-location commitments.
nodes.example: A team chooses a region near its primary users and confirms that its required database SKU is available there.

nodes.label: Datacenters
nodes.description: Datacenters provide the physical facilities, power, cooling, and networking that host Azure infrastructure.
nodes.purpose: Physical placement matters when designing for failures that can affect a building or shared facility.
nodes.example: A workload with a zone-redundancy requirement places supported resources across separate datacenters in a region.

nodes.label: Availability zones
nodes.description: Availability zones are physically separate locations within a region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking. Not every service or region supports zones.
nodes.purpose: Use zones for higher availability against a datacenter-level failure when the chosen service supports zonal or zone-redundant deployment.
nodes.example: A zone-redundant application keeps instances in multiple zones and routes requests to healthy capacity.

nodes.label: Region pairs
nodes.description: Some regions are paired for specific platform recovery and update scenarios, but pairing does not automatically replicate every resource.
nodes.purpose: Verify service-specific replication and recovery behavior instead of treating a region pair as a complete disaster-recovery plan.
nodes.example: A storage design explicitly configures geo-redundancy and tests failover rather than assuming that selecting a region creates a replica.

nodes.label: Data residency
nodes.description: Data residency requirements determine where data may be stored or processed. Service configuration, replication choice, and legal commitments all matter.
nodes.purpose: Validate the exact service and redundancy option against the organization’s policy before deployment.
nodes.example: A regulated application selects a supported in-country region and avoids a geo-replication option that would copy data outside its allowed boundary.

groups.caption: Zones protect within a region; pairs support selected recovery scenarios

title: Azure Resource Hierarchy
summary: Follow the management scope from enterprise-wide governance down to individual Azure resources.

nodes.label: Management group
nodes.description: Management groups organize subscriptions into a hierarchy so governance policies and access assignments can be inherited across subscriptions.
nodes.purpose: Use them for durable organizational policy and access boundaries that span subscriptions.
nodes.example: A platform team puts production subscriptions under a governed management group with region restrictions.

nodes.label: Subscription
nodes.description: A subscription is a billing, quota, and access-management boundary that contains resource groups and resources.
nodes.purpose: Separate subscriptions when billing, ownership, quotas, or security boundaries need clear isolation.
nodes.example: A company uses separate subscriptions for production and development, each governed by a parent management group.

nodes.label: Resource group
nodes.description: A resource group is a management container for resources that share a lifecycle or operational boundary. A resource belongs to one resource group at a time.
nodes.purpose: Group related resources for deployment, access review, policy scope, and lifecycle management.
nodes.example: An application team groups its web app, plan, and supporting service resources by environment.

nodes.label: Resource
nodes.description: A resource is an individual Azure service instance, such as a virtual machine, storage account, or virtual network.
nodes.purpose: Resource-level configuration and access assignments allow targeted administration when broader scopes are too permissive.
nodes.example: An operator assigns a narrowly scoped role on one storage account to a service team.

nodes.label: Scope inheritance
nodes.description: Azure governance scopes form a hierarchy: management group, subscription, resource group, and resource. Assignments can flow from parent scopes to descendants.
nodes.purpose: Understand inherited policy and access before troubleshooting an unexpected deny or excess access.
nodes.example: A policy assigned at a subscription applies to its resource groups and resources unless an allowed exception changes the outcome.

groups.caption: Organize subscriptions and apply policy

title: Azure Compute
summary: Choose between virtual machines, managed application platforms, event-driven compute, and containers.

nodes.label: Virtual Machines
nodes.description: Azure Virtual Machines provide configurable IaaS compute with control over the guest operating system, installed software, and runtime.
nodes.purpose: Choose a VM when operating-system control or a compatible lift-and-shift path is needed.
nodes.example: A legacy application runs on a VM while the team manages OS updates, disks, and network access.

nodes.label: Virtual Machine Scale Sets
nodes.description: Scale Sets manage a group of similarly configured VMs and can scale instance count based on rules and signals.
nodes.purpose: Use them for repeatable VM fleets that need horizontal scaling and coordinated lifecycle operations.
nodes.example: A stateless worker fleet adds instances as a queue grows and removes them as demand falls.

nodes.label: App Service
nodes.description: App Service is a managed platform for hosting web applications and APIs without managing the underlying VM operating system.
nodes.purpose: Choose it when supported runtimes and platform features meet the application’s needs.
nodes.example: A team deploys a web API to an App Service plan and uses deployment slots for staged releases.

nodes.label: Azure Functions
nodes.description: Azure Functions runs code in response to triggers such as events, timers, or queue messages, with hosting-plan-specific scaling behavior.
nodes.purpose: Use Functions for event-driven tasks and short-lived operations, while designing for retries and idempotency.
nodes.example: A function processes a message when it appears in a queue and records a result in a managed database.

nodes.label: Containers
nodes.description: Containers package an application and its dependencies into an image that can run consistently across supported environments.
nodes.purpose: Select a managed container platform based on orchestration, scaling, networking, and operational needs.
nodes.example: A team builds an image once, stores it in Azure Container Registry, then deploys it to a container service.

nodes.label: Workload requirements
nodes.description: Start with workload shape, scaling behavior, operating-system control, and how much of the runtime the team wants to manage.
nodes.purpose: Choose a compute service by operational responsibility and workload fit, then validate availability and scaling requirements.
nodes.example: A team with a custom OS image selects virtual machines; a team shipping web code may select App Service or containers.

title: Azure Networking
summary: Trace a request through virtual networks, security rules, routing, name resolution, and connectivity services.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.description: A client starts a connection using a destination name, address, protocol, and port. DNS and client-side network policy can affect the path before Azure receives traffic.
nodes.purpose: Capture the source, destination, protocol, port, and time when diagnosing connectivity.
nodes.example: An administrator compares a failed SSH attempt from a corporate network with a known-good connection from an approved jump host.

nodes.label: Virtual network
nodes.description: A virtual network is an isolated network boundary in Azure with address spaces, subnets, and connectivity options.
nodes.purpose: Plan non-overlapping address spaces and connectivity before adding peering or hybrid gateways.
nodes.example: An application VNet connects to a shared services VNet through peering and explicit routing.

nodes.label: Subnet
nodes.description: A subnet divides a VNet address range into smaller segments for placement and policy association.
nodes.purpose: Use subnets to organize workloads and apply controls such as NSGs or service endpoints.
nodes.example: Web and data workloads occupy separate subnets with different access rules.

nodes.label: NSG and routes
nodes.description: Network Security Groups allow or deny traffic using prioritized rules; routes determine the next hop for traffic.
nodes.purpose: Check effective rules and effective routes together because a valid allow rule cannot correct an incorrect route.
nodes.example: Network Watcher IP flow verify identifies an NSG deny while effective routes show the selected next hop.

nodes.label: Connectivity and endpoints
nodes.description: VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, load balancers, Azure DNS, and private endpoints solve different connectivity and traffic-management needs.
nodes.purpose: Choose a service based on trust boundary, traffic direction, availability, and whether public or private access is required.
nodes.example: A site connects over VPN Gateway while an internal application reaches a supported PaaS service through a private endpoint and DNS zone.

nodes.label: DNS resolution
nodes.description: Azure DNS can host public DNS zones, while Private DNS zones resolve names for private Azure networks. Name resolution must match the connectivity path.
nodes.purpose: Resolve the intended endpoint before troubleshooting routes or application health.
nodes.example: A VM resolves an internal service name through a linked private DNS zone before connecting over a VNet path.

nodes.label: VPN Gateway
nodes.description: VPN Gateway connects Azure virtual networks with on-premises or other networks over encrypted tunnels. Routes and address spaces must be compatible.
nodes.purpose: Use site-to-site or point-to-site connectivity when private network paths are required.
nodes.example: A branch office reaches a private application subnet through a site-to-site VPN and routes only approved address ranges.

title: Azure Storage
summary: Map common data shapes to Azure Storage services and understand where storage accounts and managed disks fit.

nodes.label: Storage account
nodes.description: A storage account is a management and namespace boundary for supported Azure Storage services and their configuration.
nodes.purpose: Choose account settings for redundancy, networking, security, and performance based on workload requirements.
nodes.example: An application uses a secured storage account with private network access and role-based data authorization.

nodes.label: Blob Storage
nodes.description: Blob Storage stores unstructured object data such as images, documents, logs, and backups.
nodes.purpose: Use access tiers and lifecycle rules to align retrieval patterns and retention requirements.
nodes.example: A media service stores uploaded images in containers and transitions older objects to a lower-access tier.

nodes.label: Azure Files
nodes.description: Azure Files provides managed file shares accessed through supported SMB or NFS protocols.
nodes.purpose: Use it when an application needs shared file-system semantics rather than object APIs.
nodes.example: Several application instances mount a common share for files that require a familiar file interface.

nodes.label: Queues and tables
nodes.description: Queue Storage provides message queues; Table Storage is a NoSQL key/attribute store for structured, non-relational data.
nodes.purpose: Use these services for simple asynchronous messaging or key-based data patterns where their semantics fit.
nodes.example: A background worker consumes queued jobs while a small lookup dataset is stored by partition and row keys.

nodes.label: Managed disks
nodes.description: Managed disks provide persistent block storage for Azure virtual machines, with performance and redundancy options.
nodes.purpose: Select disk type and size against workload I/O needs and recovery requirements.
nodes.example: A database VM uses a managed data disk sized for its expected throughput and protected by an approved backup policy.

nodes.label: Virtual machine
nodes.description: Managed disks provide persistent block storage for Azure virtual machines and are managed as separate resources from storage-account services.
nodes.purpose: Choose managed disks for VM operating-system and data volumes, with performance and redundancy matched to the workload.
nodes.example: A VM uses a premium managed disk for its database data volume while application files are stored in Blob Storage.

title: Identity and Access Management
summary: Connect identities, authentication, authorization scopes, workload identity, and secrets management.

nodes.label: Microsoft Entra ID
nodes.description: Microsoft Entra ID is the identity and access management service used to authenticate users, groups, applications, and workloads.
nodes.purpose: Centralize identity and apply sign-in protections such as multifactor authentication and Conditional Access.
nodes.example: A user signs in once and receives access to approved cloud applications based on policy.

nodes.label: Users and groups
nodes.description: Users represent people or service principals; groups collect principals so access can be assigned and reviewed consistently.
nodes.purpose: Use managed group membership and lifecycle processes instead of ad hoc user-by-user grants.
nodes.example: A project group receives a Reader role at a resource group, and membership is reviewed when the project ends.

nodes.label: Azure RBAC
nodes.description: Azure RBAC authorizes actions on Azure resources using role definitions, assignments, principals, and scopes.
nodes.purpose: Grant the minimum required role at the narrowest scope and distinguish management-plane roles from data-plane roles.
nodes.example: A support engineer receives VM Reader access on one resource group rather than subscription-wide Contributor access.

nodes.label: Managed identity
nodes.description: A managed identity gives an Azure workload an Entra identity whose credentials are managed by the platform.
nodes.purpose: Use it to obtain tokens for supported services without embedding long-lived credentials in application settings.
nodes.example: An App Service managed identity receives a narrowly scoped data role on a storage account.

nodes.label: Key Vault
nodes.description: Key Vault stores and controls access to secrets, keys, and certificates used by applications and operators.
nodes.purpose: Use identity-based access, least privilege, audit, and network controls to protect sensitive values.
nodes.example: A deployment retrieves a required certificate through an approved workload identity rather than committing it to source control.

title: Monitoring and Observability
summary: Follow telemetry from an application through Azure Monitor to logs, alerts, and operator action.

nodes.label: Application
nodes.description: Applications emit telemetry about requests, dependencies, traces, and exceptions that can explain user-visible behavior.
nodes.purpose: Instrument key user journeys and correlate telemetry with deployments while avoiding secrets and unnecessary personal data.
nodes.example: A request trace shows that a web endpoint spends most of its response time waiting for a database dependency.

nodes.label: Azure Monitor
nodes.description: Azure Monitor collects and analyzes supported metrics and logs from Azure resources and applications.
nodes.purpose: Use it to build dashboards, query telemetry, and configure alert rules for operational signals.
nodes.example: An operator compares a rising error rate with CPU and dependency metrics to locate a bottleneck.

nodes.label: Metrics and logs
nodes.description: Metrics are numeric time series; logs are records that can be queried for detailed events and correlation.
nodes.purpose: Choose the signal that answers the question: fast aggregated health or detailed event investigation.
nodes.example: A metric alert detects a latency threshold while a KQL query correlates failed requests with application traces.

nodes.label: Alerts and action groups
nodes.description: Alert rules evaluate metrics or logs and can notify people or invoke configured actions through action groups.
nodes.purpose: Make alerts actionable, scoped, and tested to reduce noise and ensure the right responder is notified.
nodes.example: A log alert opens an incident when repeated application errors exceed a validated threshold.

nodes.label: Operator response
nodes.description: Operators use Azure Monitor alongside Service Health and Resource Health to distinguish workload issues from platform events.
nodes.purpose: Correlate impact, scope, timeline, recent changes, and dependencies before changing production resources.
nodes.example: A team checks Service Health for a regional incident while inspecting application traces for a separate database timeout.

nodes.label: Application Insights
nodes.description: Application Insights collects application telemetry such as requests, dependencies, exceptions, and traces for application-level diagnosis.
nodes.purpose: Use application telemetry to connect user symptoms with service behavior and downstream dependencies.
nodes.example: A latency investigation correlates slow requests with a database dependency and exception traces.

title: Governance and Security
summary: Use policy, locks, security posture tools, and compliance evidence as complementary controls.

nodes.label: Azure Policy
nodes.description: Azure Policy evaluates resource configuration against organizational rules and can audit, deny, or support remediation.
nodes.purpose: Use policy to express required configuration consistently across governance scopes.
nodes.example: A policy audits storage accounts that permit public access before the organization considers enforcement.

nodes.label: Resource locks
nodes.description: Resource locks help protect supported resources from accidental deletion or modification at a chosen scope.
nodes.purpose: Use locks as an additional guardrail, and verify that automation and approved maintenance account for them.
nodes.example: A critical resource group receives a deletion-prevention lock while change processes remain responsible for data protection.

nodes.label: Defender for Cloud
nodes.description: Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides security posture management and workload protection capabilities for supported environments.
nodes.purpose: Use recommendations as signals to investigate and prioritize risks; validate changes against workload needs.
nodes.example: A security team reviews a public management endpoint finding, confirms ownership, and narrows access through an approved change.

nodes.label: Compliance and data governance
nodes.description: Compliance work maps organizational and regulatory obligations to controls, responsibilities, and evidence. Microsoft Purview supports data governance and compliance-related capabilities.
nodes.purpose: Treat compliance as a shared operating process; a cloud certification does not automatically make a customer workload compliant.
nodes.example: A team documents data classification, retention, identity controls, and evidence for its workload boundary.

nodes.label: Defense in depth
nodes.description: Defense in depth layers identity, network, host, application, data, and monitoring controls so a single failure is less likely to expose a workload.
nodes.purpose: Review controls together and test their interactions rather than depending on one perimeter rule.
nodes.example: A service combines least-privilege identity, private connectivity, encryption, logging, and tested recovery.

nodes.label: Azure resource estate
nodes.description: The resource estate is the set of subscriptions and services governed by organizational policies and security controls.
nodes.purpose: Establish governance and security controls at the right scopes before teams deploy workloads.
nodes.example: A platform team applies allowed-region policies and security baselines to subscriptions used by application teams.

title: Cost Management
summary: Trace Azure cost from workload choices to budgets, analysis, and operational optimization.

nodes.label: Usage and pricing factors
nodes.description: Azure costs can depend on region, service tier, usage duration, storage, data transfer, licensing, and enabled features.
nodes.purpose: Estimate using workload assumptions and review actual usage after deployment; avoid relying on memorized prices.
nodes.example: A VM estimate includes its size and runtime, disk configuration, backup, public IP, and expected outbound transfer.

nodes.label: Cost analysis
nodes.description: Cost Management cost analysis groups and filters usage and charges across supported billing and resource scopes.
nodes.purpose: Use time comparisons and dimensions such as service, resource, meter, and tags to explain a change.
nodes.example: An unexpected monthly increase is traced to a new logging workspace and a data-ingestion increase.

nodes.label: Budgets and alerts
nodes.description: Budgets track actual or forecast spending against thresholds and can send notifications; they do not automatically stop consumption.
nodes.purpose: Configure alerts with owners and response steps, and understand reporting delay and billing scope.
nodes.example: A forecasted-cost alert prompts a team to inspect a planned scale-out before its monthly review.

nodes.label: Tags and allocation
nodes.description: Tags are metadata that can help organize resources and allocate costs by owner, environment, product, or cost center.
nodes.purpose: Standardize and enforce tag keys; tags do not provide access control and may not cover every bill item.
nodes.example: A policy requires environment and service-owner tags on new resources so cost reports can be grouped consistently.

nodes.label: Optimization choices
nodes.description: Optimization can include right-sizing, removing idle resources, scheduling nonproduction workloads, and evaluating commitments for stable usage.
nodes.purpose: Validate recommendations against performance, resilience, and recovery objectives before applying them.
nodes.example: A team schedules a nonproduction VM to stop overnight while retaining its disks and checking application dependencies.
